output.title: The Cutting of the String
output.prologue: We are the Gulls, and the news between Vel, the Upper Sea, and the islands is ours to carry. We were wet and hungry the morning the string was cut, and we have carried the news ever since, from cliff to cloud and back. This is the telling as we heard it on the wind. Follow us from star to star. Each hop is short, the way a gull flies, and each stop is a thing you can hold: a spindle, a bowl, a boat, a bird. Keep count as you go. Hesk does.

stops.text: At the pole Mother Hesk sat with her spindle, drawing the string out thin and winding it on the whorl so the islands would not drift. We were her messengers then, and she sent us down each morning with a count of knots. Then Aun came up the cliff with his knife in his belt and a question in his mouth. Hesk did not look up. She kept her hands on the thread, because a spindle that stops is a string that falls.

Aun drew the knife across the string, and the sky went up off the islands like a sail let loose. We saw it from the wind. The shore birds on the cliffs felt the pull go out of their feet, and they had nothing left to wind. Gulls screamed at the edge of the drift. Hesk saw the cut and kept count anyway, as she does, because a thing that has been counted is not wholly lost. She marked the knot where the string parted.

Aun was thirsty when the sky went up, as Fliers are, having shouted all day at the wind. He had no bottle, so he shouted again, and the wind took his words up after the kites. We gulls were sent down with the news that the Flier had gone dry. Nobody on the shingle laughed, though Tavo did, from far off, where the spray came down like cold salt. Aun licked his wrist and called it weather.

The sky ran up so fast the year's sailcloth nearly tore from the Reel. Hesk was quick. She put her hand to the loom weight and held the cloth down, the way she holds a child's hem in a squall. Then she sent us: the string is cut, the sky is loose, and the Reel is pulling. We went down the cliffs in a rush of white feathers, shouting it to every ledge the cold wind reached.

When the string was cut, the wind carried the messages Vel had sent down to the islands, and gulls were the ones who carried them back. One grey gull from the Leeward stacks was carrying a word when the wind tore it loose. She could not hold it. Now the word is somewhere over the Upper Sea, and every grieving house asks the gulls for it. We tell them we are looking. We are still looking.

Boats in the Leeward Reach lost their way the night the sky drifted off. There was no light to steer by, only the wet dark and the wind coming round. Hesk counted the missing from her pole, and the count came out wrong, and she was not pleased. Hesk is patient with everything but a count that will not close. Tallow lamps were lit on every cliff. We flew over them, carrying the count from door to door.

A boat went out past the Leeward edge in the year the herring failed. Her name was painted on the stern in old red, and the sea took the paint before it took the boat. Now she goes aloft with no name. We gulls looked for the name on the wind and found only a red smear. Kael casts for lamps like hers, though he never hauls one up. We cannot read a name off the wind, so we say it instead, every one we remember.

When the string was cut, the drowned began going aloft by sea, and the sea would not give them back. Kael the Netter casts for them every night off the Leeward edge. We have watched his net go out black and come back with nothing but salt and a little weed. Still he casts. The sea keeps its own count, and the lamps of the drowned hang over the water like a boat's lights in the mist.

When Aun cut the string, the sky went up, and the dead went with it as kites. But the Unflown lies past where the wind comes back, and there the dead do not stay tied. We carry no word from there. Only the cords hang loose. Old fishers say a rope with no mooring still gives a warning in a gale, and the Unlaid Rope hums in the deep south when the sea is calm.

When Aun cut the string, the sky went up and the ladder did not. Ennu had knotted it that spring from goat gut and whale-rib rungs, and it hung from the cliff-neck over the Unflown water. Aun had meant to climb back down by it. Instead he climbed nothing. The rungs still hang there, swinging a little when the wind goes south, and gulls are glad to perch on the lowest one.

Aun built a boat of cloth and bone and sailed it south, past the last island, because he wanted to see where the wind stopped. The water tilted under him. We followed for a while, dipping and crying, until the swell grew too long for wings. Ennu had sewn the sail, and Aun had lashed the bones with gut, and the hull went down the dark slope of the sea, and the wake turned back on itself.

Óllun was a sailor who asked the wind where it stopped. He took his boat south, past the last of the kelp, until the water went smooth and dark and the stars were wrong. Then his boat turned back on its own. Some say Aun's wake turned him. We think he had the answer and did not want it. He came home quiet and would not tell the wind what he had seen.

When Aun cut the string he did not know that a sky has weight. Tavo the Gale came in under the drift and lifted the first boats clean off the water. Ennu thought he had made the drift light enough, and he had not. We saw the lantern boats climb like kites on a line, their crews hanging over the gunwales, and the sea below them empty and shining. Tavo laughed at the weight.

A girl of the Holm house went down to the shingle with her brother's box-kite, new, bone-framed and bright with sailcloth. The wind took it out of her fists and carried it past the rocks toward the Leeward dark. She did not cry. She stood on the stones with her hands still shaped to the string, and we gulls came down beside her to see what she would do next.

Ennu the Kite-Wright made a gull once, of sailcloth and goose-bone, and gave it to a girl on the windward cliff who had asked the wind a question and got no answer. The gull was tied to her wrist with a short line. She held it up into the north wind, and it pulled, and pulled, and did not go. That is the only answer the wind gives to most questions. We gulls know it well.

Skeru was a raven who sat on the highest stake of Hesk's Reel and put questions to the wind all day. Is the herring running? Is the goat-boy home? Where does the string go? We are told she still asks. Hesk does not answer her either, but she winds every question into the count, so none is lost. The gulls carry them up and down, and this is where our telling ends, with a question still open.
